extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, literary critics, and students of poetics (writers of drama and narrative)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and evaluative principles for composing and judging poetic works (especially tragedy and epic): addresses imitation (mimesis), the medium/objects/manner of imitation, the six elements of tragedy, plot construction (unity, reversal, recognition), character, diction, thought, and related compositional rules and objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation (mimesis) as the organizing principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and allied arts are modes of imitation; imitation is the common principle of the arts of poetry, music, dancing, painting, and sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing, treat the work as an imitation of human action or life; choose what to imitate and how, keeping in mind the aims and effects of imitation rather than mere copying of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium of imitation: rhythm, language, harmony (melody)
rubrics_metrics.description: The medium or material vehicle of imitation is rhythm, language, and 'harmony' (or melody), taken singly or combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and control metre/rhythm, linguistic style, and musical elements appropriately to the form (e.g., epic, lyric, drama). Misuse (e.g., inappropriate metre for tone) weakens the imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation: higher or lower types
rubrics_metrics.description: Works differ in the kinds of persons/objects they represent (higher or lower types); in poetry this underpins distinctions like Tragedy vs Comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose whether to represent elevated characters and actions (tragedy) or lower/comic types; the moral and intellectual level of characters should suit the genre and intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner (mode) of imitation: dramatic, narrative, lyric
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry may be in form either dramatic narrative, pure narrative (including lyric), or pure drama; the manner of imitation is a fundamental distinguishing feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to show action directly (dramatic), tell it (narrative), or combine modes; mixing modes must be done for clear artistic reasons and not confuse unity of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six elements of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy has six constituent elements: Spectacle (opsis), Song/Lyrical element (melos), Diction (lexis), Plot (mythos), Character (ethos), and Thought (dianoia). Plot is primary; character and thought come next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate or compose tragedy by ensuring these six elements are present and integrated, with special attention to plot as the organizing principle and to how diction and song serve the plot and characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as the primary element: a whole with magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot must be a Whole, complete in itself, and of a certain magnitude (proper size and complexity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft plots with a clear beginning, middle, and end so the action is unified and of suitable length to accomplish its emotional/intellectual effect; overly long or fragmented plots dilute impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (dramatic unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of Plot consists not in unity of hero but in unity of action; the parts must be organically connected and form one complete action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid episodic or disconnected incidents; every episode should contribute causally to the single central action. Anti-pattern: plots assembled from unrelated episodes ('bag of adventures').

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of probable or necessary sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidents must follow from each other by probability or necessity; the sequence should be coherent and causally connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the chain of events appear natural within the world of the play; improbable juxtapositions without artistic justification break the plot's credibility. Prefer necessary sequence when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best tragic effect: combination of the inevitable and the unexpected
rubrics_metrics.description: The finest tragic effects combine what is inevitable with what is unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for outcomes that, once revealed, seem necessary (inevitable) yet include moments of surprise (recognition, reversal) that strengthen emotional impact. Avoid outcomes that feel arbitrary or telegraphed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs complex plots; components: reversal, recognition, suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex plots involve reversal of intention (peripeteia), recognition (anagnorisis), and tragic or disastrous incidents (pathos); simple plots lack these structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reversal and recognition to intensify catharsis; ensure such elements arise organically from the plot rather than by contrivance. A simple plot may still be effective but uses fewer structural turns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (reversal) and anagnorisis (recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal of intention is a change to the opposite in the agent's situation; recognition is the change from ignorance to knowledge (or vice versa). Both are key mechanisms by which plot produces tragic emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure events so that a character's position changes logically and poignantly; recognition should be motivated and believable (not arbitrary revelation). These moments should deepen pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathos (tragic suffering) as integral incident
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic or disastrous incidents (pathos) are moments of suffering that should arise from the plot and character rather than from spectacle alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure scenes of suffering emerge from causal sequence and character choice; avoid manufactured shocks purely for sensational effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative parts (structural divisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy has quantitative parts such as Prologue, Episodes, Chorus, and Exode (and other formal divisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organise the work into clear parts that serve the whole action; each part should have a defined role (e.g., prologue sets up action, episodes advance it, choral odes reflect and integrate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of fortune must arise from character and action
rubrics_metrics.description: The change of fortune (peripeteia) should proceed from the structure of the action and from the character's choices/traits rather than random chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make causes of reversal intelligible in character terms; the protagonist's moral qualities and errors should plausibly lead to consequences. Avoid deus ex machina that resolves or produces outcomes without organic cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for unhappy/tragic endings over 'poetic justice' when true to tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: An unhappy ending is more truly tragic than tidy 'poetic justice' favored by popular taste; tragedy aims at a particular kind of emotional and intellectual effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an ending that best serves the tragic unity and catharsis rather than simply restoring moral order for audience comfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pity and fear must arise from the plot rather than spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic emotions of pity and fear should spring out of the Plot itself; to produce them by scenery or spectacular effect is against the spirit of Tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on narrative causation and moral dynamics to elicit emotion; anti-pattern: using scenery, special effects, or gratuitous shock to manufacture pity/fear without structural justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character as manifestation of moral purpose with probability and necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is the manifestation of moral purpose and must conform to the rules of necessity or probability; characters should be consistent and credible within the work's universe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portrait characters ethically and psychologically plausibly; avoid characters acting out of inconsistent motives. Idealise character only insofar as it suits the poet's end and the plot's needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deus ex machina
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolutions that depend on arbitrary divine intervention or an exterior contrivance to solve the plot are improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclude the action through causes implicit in the plot and character; avoid external contrivances that break the unity and credibility of the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical composing rules for the tragic poet
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical directions include: place the scene before your eyes and act the parts yourself to enter into sympathy with the dramatis personae; sketch the bare outline of the action before filling in episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use embodiment and enactment to test plausibility; prepare an outline to preserve unity and causal connection before elaborating details. Anti-pattern: improvising episodes without an outline leads to incoherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful treatment of complication (dépos) and dénouement
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful about the complication and the dénouement of the plot, especially the dénouement, since these determine the effect and coherence of the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure complications develop naturally and the dénouement resolves or reveals in ways true to the plot's causal logic; sloppy dénouements dilute catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of chorus and episodic material (choral odes organic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the Choral Odes—like the Dialogue—an organic part of the whole action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use choral odes to reflect, heighten, or thematise the action rather than as digressive spectacles; anti-pattern: choral material that interrupts or contradicts the plot's flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia) and diction (lexis) as conveyors of idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the intellectual element revealed in speeches composed according to rhetoric; diction is the particular words and style, and largely concerns delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose speeches so that thought is clear and rhetorically effective; select diction that matches character, tone, and audience comprehension—elevated yet lucid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic diction and permissible figures (including metaphor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic diction has permitted modes of speech, including metaphors; poetry should combine elevation of language with perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ metaphor and elevated language when they clarify or amplify meaning; avoid obscurity for its own sake. Balance ornament with intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form-specific differences (Epic vs Tragedy): length, metre, plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic and Tragedy agree in unity of action but differ in length, metre, and the art of imparting a plausible air to incredible fiction; Epic's length dilutes concentrated effect that Tragedy achieves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose form according to desired scope: epic for extensive, many-part actions; tragedy for concentrated unified action. Be mindful that expansive length can reduce unity and intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to critical objections: five sources of censure
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical objections usually derive from: impossibility, irrationality, moral harm, contradiction, or breach of artistic correctness; answers should be sought under twelve heads (e.g., artistic requirement, higher reality, common opinion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When confronted with objections, justify departures from mundane plausibility by reference to artistic necessity, ideal types, or received opinion; prefer a probable impossibility justified by art to an improbable possibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles for textual interpretation and resolving difficulties
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguities or apparent inconsistencies in language may be resolved by metaphor, accent/breathing, punctuation, ambiguity of construction, or usage; critics should avoid assuming groundless conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting texts or composing ambiguous lines, consider multiple linguistic and rhetorical solutions rather than hastily judging inconsistency. Anti-pattern: critics inventing errors based on preconceptions.
